name: Outdoors & sea
desc: Rip currents, jellyfish, sea urchins, weever fish, snakes, stings, cold, getting lost, signalling

s: Stay calm: a rip pulls you out, not under.
If you can stand, wade out instead of swimming.
Don't swim straight back against it. Swim parallel to the beach until you're out of the pull, then head for shore.
Too tired? Float on your back and let it take you; rips often loop back towards shallower water.
Raise one hand and shout for help.
Seeing someone else in trouble: alert a lifeguard or call 112. Throw something that floats instead of swimming in.
Get out of the water.
Rinse the area with seawater.
Remove any tentacles with tweezers or the edge of a card, not with bare hands.
For the pain: a cold pack wrapped in a cloth, or paracetamol.
Call 112 if they have trouble breathing, chest pain, a big swelling or feel very unwell.
d: No fresh water: it makes the stinging cells fire
No vinegar for Mediterranean jellyfish (like the purple Pelagia): it can make it worse
Don't rub the skin or put sand on it
guides.src: Research on Mediterranean jellyfish (Pelagia noctiluca) stings

s: Move away from the snake and keep the person calm. Many bites are ‘dry’ (no venom).
Let them sit or lie down and keep still.
Keep the bitten arm or leg still, like in a splint or sling.
Take off rings, watches and tight clothing near the bite: it will swell.
Call 112 or go to the nearest hospital. Mark the edge of the swelling with a pen and the time.
Paracetamol is fine for the pain.
d: Don't cut, suck or burn the bite
Don't try to catch or kill the snake

s: Bee sting: scrape the sting out sideways with a fingernail or card.
Wash, then cool with a cold pack.
Watch for 30 minutes for signs of an allergic reaction: swelling of face or throat, trouble breathing, dizziness.
Any of those: call 112 and see “Severe allergic reaction”.
d: Don't squeeze the sting out with tweezers

guides.w: Very cold, shivering, confused or sleepy
s: Get them out of the wind and wet, into shelter.
Replace wet clothes with dry ones; insulate from the ground; cover the head.
Warm them slowly with blankets and body heat.
If they're fully awake: warm sweet drinks.
Severe (very drowsy, stopped shivering, confused): call 112 and handle them gently.
d: Don't rub their skin or put them in a hot bath

guides.w: You don't know where you are
s: Stop, stay calm and stay where you are if people know your plan: it's easier to find someone who doesn't move.
Open the app's map: your GPS works without internet if you downloaded the area.
Share your position: SMS your coordinates or call 112.
No phone: the sun rises in the east and sets in the west; at midday in Europe it's in the south.
Stay warm and visible: bright clothing, an open spot.
Three of anything means ‘help’: 3 whistle blasts, 3 flashes, 3 shouts, repeated.
SOS with a torch or phone light: 3 short, 3 long, 3 short.
Make yourself big and bright: wave clothing, use a mirror or phone screen to flash sunlight.
At night: a steady or flashing light from an open spot.
Get out of the water and sit down.
Pull out spines you can grip easily with tweezers, straight out.
Soak the foot in water as hot as you can comfortably stand (not scalding) for 30–90 minutes: it eases the pain.
Clean it with soap and water or disinfectant.
See a doctor if spines are deep, near a joint, or the spot gets red, swollen or warm after a few days.
d: Don't dig for deep spines with a needle or knife

guides.w: Sudden sharp pain in the foot on a sandy beach
s: Very sharp, burning pain after stepping on something in shallow water on a sandy beach: probably a weever fish.
Put the foot in water as hot as you can comfortably stand (around 40–45 °C) for 30–90 minutes. The heat breaks the poison down.
Top up with hot water as it cools. Painkillers can help.
Remove any small spines you can see.
Call 112 if they get short of breath, dizzy or swollen elsewhere. See a doctor if the pain lasts or it gets infected.
Wear water shoes on sandy beaches in summer, also on the Dutch coast.
d: Don't use ice: it makes the pain worse
